subtitleEn: This day is light and joy for Israel
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | A A | Dm Dm |
metaLine: 88 BPM · 4/4 · Friday night, and one of the best-loved tunes in the whole repertoire · eleven short stanzas, each ending on the same two words
intro: Two words close every stanza and open the song: Sabbath of rest. Eleven stanzas, three lines each, and the last line of every one lands on that phrase — which is why a table can sing this for ten minutes with only three words of Hebrew between them. The tune is one of the most loved in the Ashkenazi repertoire and is often hummed long after the words have run out.

stanzas.label: refrain

lines.en: This day for Israel is light and joy: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: Seven words that come back as the opening of the song and, in their last two, as the close of every stanza. {{0.3}} and {{0.4}} — light and joy — are from Esther, where they describe what the Jews had when the decree was lifted.

stanzas.label: at Sinai

lines.en: You commanded precepts at the standing at Sinai,
the Sabbath and the festivals, to keep all my years,
to set before me an offering and a prepared meal: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{1.2}} is the standing at Sinai, the fixed Hebrew name for that scene. The stanza moves from a mountain to a laid table in three lines, which is the poem's habit.

stanzas.label: the extra soul

lines.en: The desire of hearts for a broken people,
for pained souls, an additional soul;
from a soul in distress He will remove sighing: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{5.2}} and {{5.3}} are the additional soul — the Talmudic idea that a person receives an extra soul for the day and loses it when the day ends. This is the stanza the tune is usually saddest on.

lines.en: You sanctified it and blessed it above all days,
in six You completed the work of worlds;
on it the grieving found quiet and trust: a Sabbath of rest.
For the prohibition of work You commanded us, Awesome One;
may I merit the splendour of kingship, if I keep the Sabbath;
I will offer a gift to the Awesome One, an offering of spices: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.label: a song for You

lines.en: And a song I will arrange for You, with melody and sweetness,
before the beauty of Your greatness my soul has longed for You;
for a whole treasured people, fulfil the promise: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{13.3}} is the word for a melody without words, the niggun. The poem names its own performance: a song arranged with a tune, being sung at the table it describes.

stanzas.label: accept my prayer

lines.en: Accept my prayer like the offering of Nachshon,
and on the day of my rest, in joy and gladness;
beloved as the pupil of an eye, with much success: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{16.4}} is Nachshon ben Aminadav, the prince of Judah who brought the first offering at the dedication of the Tabernacle in Numbers 7 — and, in the midrash, the first man into the sea. Named here without explanation, as these poems always do.

lines.en: For Your salvation we have hoped, God, mightiest of the mighty;
son of David our king, send now to the blind,
and He will proclaim freedom, relief and ease: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.label: please, answer us

lines.en: Please, exalted and awesome One, look and answer us;
redeem us quickly, be gracious to us and answer us;
gladden our soul with light and joy: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: Four imperatives in two lines, all addressed to God, all in the plural — look, answer, redeem, be gracious. The stanza before this one asked on behalf of the blind; this one asks on behalf of everyone at the table.

stanzas.label: renew the sanctuary

lines.en: Renew our sanctuary; remember the ruined city;
Your goodness, our Saviour, give to the grieving woman
who sits on the Sabbath in song and praise: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{25.3}} and {{26.3}} are both feminine — the ruined city and the grieving woman are the same figure, Jerusalem, which Hebrew treats as a woman throughout the prophets.

stanzas.label: remember for us

lines.en: Remember for us, Holy One, by the merit of the preciousness of the day;
guard us, please, on this day and on every day;
my Beloved, bright and awesome, bring relief: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: {{30.0}}, {{30.1}} and {{30.2}} — my beloved, bright and ruddy — is from the Song of Songs, and using it as a name for God is standard in this poetry and startling the first time you meet it.

stanzas.label: let it be heard

lines.en: A voice of song and salvation, let it be heard for Israel,
when the vision of deliverance comes, the Rock who makes salvation grow;
light of my sun, appear, shine always: a Sabbath of rest.

stanzas.summary: The poem ends on the sun, which is where a Friday night song about light should end — and on the same two words that have closed every stanza since the first.

chantTips: The two closing words are the whole song for a guest. They arrive at the end of every stanza, and a table will land on them together whether or not anyone knows the verses.
Slower than most: around 88 BPM. The melody is worth taking time over and is often hummed after the words stop.
Three lines per stanza, and the third is always longer — it carries the refrain words. Give it room.
Twelve stanzas is more than most tables sing. Four or five is normal; the tune usually outlasts the text.

about.body: The opening letters of the stanzas spell the name Yitzchak. Which Yitzchak is not established, and the poem is usually dated by its style rather than by any external record.

The third stanza names the neshamah yeterah, the extra soul the Talmud says a person receives for the Sabbath and loses when it ends. That idea is why havdalah uses spices — to revive the ordinary soul left behind — and this poem is one of the places a learner is most likely to meet it.

The melody now sung across the Ashkenazi world is later than the words and is one of the most recognisable in the repertoire. It is not reproduced here; the chord grid is a suggestion for accompanying it, not a transcription of it.
